strengths: Addresses a timely and important privacy vulnerability in agentic multi-modal LLMs during their rapid deployment
Novel problem formulation: first systematic investigation of inference-stage privacy leakage through image geolocation
Clear and well-structured methodology with comprehensive empirical analysis of 50 privacy-sensitive images
Concrete findings with street-level accuracy (60% within 1 mile) and systematic identification of critical visual cues for geolocation
Thorough categorization of 30+ visual elements contributing to location inference with targeted occlusion experiments
Realistic threat model based on actual doxing scenarios from public social media
Excellent presentation with detailed example interactions demonstrating model reasoning process
weaknesses: Dataset size of only 50 images is insufficient for strong statistical claims and generalizability to broader population
Exclusive focus on ChatGPT o3 without evaluation on other agentic multi-modal models (GPT-4V, Claude, Gemini), limiting understanding of generality
Severely limited geographic scope (only major U.S. cities + few international locations) reduces applicability to different urban architectures and regions
Missing critical baselines: no human performance comparison, no comparison with simpler geolocation methods, no model component ablations
Incomplete evaluation of defense mechanisms: only one detailed masking experiment shown; insufficient systematic evaluation of obfuscation effectiveness
No statistical rigor: lacking confidence intervals, significance testing, cross-validation, or hold-out test sets
Reproducibility impossible: dataset not publicly available (even anonymized), limited prompt engineering details, no code released
Limited technical novelty: primarily an empirical security audit without new methods, algorithms, or theoretical contributions
Insufficient prompt sensitivity analysis: Figure 3 shows different prompts but lacks systematic ablation study on prompt effects
Incomplete ethical treatment: limited discussion of responsible disclosure timeline or broader societal implications of findings

strengths: Addresses an important and timely privacy vulnerability in agentic multi-modal LLMs
Systematic and well-structured experimental workflow with clear data collection and analysis phases
Detailed feature analysis identifying which visual cues (street layout, front yard design) enable geolocation
Concrete real-world demonstrations effectively illustrating practical doxing risks
Appropriate scope for targeted investigation with interpretable results
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset (only 50 images) with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or generalizability analysis
Complete absence of baselines: no comparison to other vision-language models, no human baseline, no comparison to alternative geolocation approaches
Limited technical novelty: purely empirical black-box evaluation with no novel methods, algorithms, or theoretical insights
Insufficient analysis depth: only one masking defense tested, no investigation of failure cases, arbitrary distance thresholds, limited ablation studies
Reproducibility concerns: dataset cannot be released, results tied to proprietary model, insufficient implementation details
Privacy leakage from LLMs/MLLMs is well-established in prior work; this applies that finding to geolocation without fundamental advance
No responsible disclosure discussion and detailed exploitation examples could enable malicious doxing
Reads as security red team report rather than novel research contribution meeting top-tier venue standards

strengths: Novel and timely focus on privacy leakage through image geolocation in agentic MLLMs, addressing an emerging vulnerability not previously systematically studied
Well-designed empirical methodology using real-world images with ground truth locations across diverse U.S. cities and states, providing more credible findings than synthetic data
Clear and compelling quantitative results (60% within 1 mile, 84% within 5 miles) with meaningful distance-based metrics that map to real privacy risks
Comprehensive fine-grained analysis identifying key visual cues (street layout, front yard design) that contribute to model predictions, with detailed categorization of visual elements
Strong presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 7-13) and detailed case studies in appendix showing model reasoning chains and behaviors
Concrete demonstration that simple masking is insufficient, suggesting need for stronger privacy-preserving defenses in multimodal systems
Rigorous manual dataset construction with diverse geographic coverage and careful attention to ethical considerations
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale (50 images) and geographic scope (U.S. only, primarily suburban residences with visible individuals), raising questions about generalization to other regions, image types, and privacy-relevant scenarios

Single model evaluation—no comparison with other MLLMs (GPT-4V, Claude Vision, LLaVA) or traditional geolocation methods, preventing assessment of whether vulnerability is specific to ChatGPT o3 or more general
Dataset cannot be released due to privacy and licensing concerns, significantly limiting reproducibility and community ability to verify or extend findings
Incomplete analysis of defense mechanisms—masking experiments test only one approach and lack quantitative results on how much accuracy is reduced; other privacy-preserving techniques not explored
Minimal statistical rigor with no confidence intervals, significance tests, error analysis, or examination of prediction confidence/uncertainty
Missing failure case analysis—no investigation of what prevents the model from geolocating certain images, limiting understanding of vulnerability scope
Methodological gaps including somewhat ad-hoc selection of four prompt types without systematic exploration of prompt engineering effects on geolocation capability

Narrow scope focused on residential locations of people in front of homes; unclear how findings apply to other privacy-sensitive scenarios (workplaces, infrastructure) or images without visible individuals

strengths: Identifies important, timely, and overlooked privacy vulnerability in MLRMs with clear legal/policy implications (GDPR/CCPA)
Comprehensive evaluation across 11 diverse models (open/closed-source MLRMs and MLLMs) with multiple metrics and settings
High-quality, carefully curated DOXBENCH dataset (500 images) addressing key gaps in existing Street View-based datasets with three-level privacy framework
Novel and well-motivated evaluation metrics: VRR appropriately captures refusal behavior; GLARE is theoretically grounded information-theoretic measure combining multiple dimensions
Strong analytical insights: 98% human agreement on clue-based reasoning; CLUEMINER extracts 102 interpretable clue categories; clear evidence models lack privacy-aligned mechanisms
Realistic threat modeling with GEOMINER collaborative attack framework and human-model comparisons (15-21× better performance)
Honest assessment of defense limitations with clear mechanistic analysis of failure modes
Well-written paper with clear visualization and solid organization
weaknesses: Limited geographic scope (California only, 6 cities) with unclear generalization to other regions/countries; raises concerns about regional bias in model training interactions
Modest dataset size (500 images) and methodological concerns: only 5 human participants, no confidence intervals/significance testing, IQR filtering without justification
Concurrent work (refs [3-5], [21-22]) addresses similar location-leakage problems; while differentiation is meaningful, core novelty is somewhat incremental
CLUEMINER limitations: depends on GPT-4O for category analysis (potential bias), applied only to correct predictions (selection bias), no inter-annotator agreement validation
Tool-augmented evaluation based on only 10 manually selected 'challenging' cases per risk level—may not be representative and could overstate threat severity
Defense discussion lacks depth: only one guardrail tested, no post-training fine-tuning strategies discussed, utility-privacy tradeoffs not fully quantified, no forward-looking solutions
DOXBENCH not publicly available limiting reproducibility; code availability not mentioned; confined to those with model API access
Statistical rigor issues: no formal significance testing, selection biases in subgroup analyses (e.g., mirror cases only 46 images), Top-K evaluation somewhat artificial

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem of location privacy leakage in MLRMs with genuine real-world implications
Introduces DOXBENCH, a novel dataset of 500 real-world images with three privacy risk levels, improving upon prior work's low-resolution Street View data
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 11 advanced models (6 MLRMs, 5 MLLMs) with multiple evaluation dimensions
Multiple innovative analytical frameworks: CLUEMINER for systematic clue extraction (102 categories), GEOMINER for collaborative attack scenarios
Systematic analysis of clue-based reasoning with convergent evidence from human evaluation (98%) and LLM-as-judge (97.7%)
Information-theoretic evaluation metric (GLARE) that unifies response likelihood and spatial accuracy
Honest discussion of defense limitations, acknowledging that perturbation and prompt-based approaches face fundamental challenges
weaknesses: Critical geographic limitation: All 500 images from California only, severely undermining generalizability claims and rendering 'real-world threat' narrative questionable without cross-regional validation

Modest dataset size (500 images) with significant imbalance across risk levels (L1: 126, L2: 186, L3: 186); only 46 mirror cases and 10 tool-augmented samples per risk level insufficient for robust conclusions

GLARE metric is convoluted and unintuitive: lacks validation against human privacy intuitions, unclear what 1800 vs. 1900 bits means practically, and geometric mean choice for d50/d̄ combination unjustified

CLUEMINER methodology is ad-hoc: no validation of 102 discovered categories, no inter-rater reliability studies, convergence at sample 552 with unexplored sensitivity to input ordering, and model-bias from using O4-MINI as analyzer

Pervasive lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; human comparison on only 5 undergrad CS students and 30 images; no reporting of standard deviations across runs

Threat model overclaimed: (1) '21× better than humans' is misleading (humans achieved 9.5km MED vs. models' 4-5km), conflates AED with MED, (2) real-world attack scenarios unclear, (3) GEOMINER requires strategic multi-step queries with unclear practical applicability

Insufficient defense analysis: only Gaussian noise tested for perturbation, LLAMA GUARD4 failure not deeply analyzed, prompt-based defenses lack utility-privacy tradeoff characterization, incomplete for responsible AI venue
Missing critical ablations: no ablation on three-level privacy framework, GLARE metric components, or systematic prompt variation studies

Limited methodological justification: 300-second human time limit arbitrary, CoT prompt elaborateness may bias comparisons, outlier filtering with IQR methodology vague, model selection criteria not explained

strengths: Addresses a timely and important privacy vulnerability in MLRMs that has received limited attention despite widespread deployment
Comprehensive evaluation across 11 diverse models (6 MLRMs, 5 MLLMs) with both open-source and closed-source options
High-quality DOXBENCH dataset (500 real images, 3 privacy risk levels) that substantially improves upon prior work using low-resolution Street View or landmark-only images
Novel GLARE metric combining information theory with geolocation accuracy, providing principled way to quantify privacy leakage
Strong analytical framework identifying clue-based reasoning as key mechanism, validated by human evaluation (98%) and LLM-as-Judge (97.7%)
CLUEMINER discovers and categorizes 102 visual clue types, revealing models lack privacy-aligned mechanisms to suppress sensitive clues
Realistic attack scenarios demonstrating both tool-augmented reasoning (O3 with web search: 49% GLARE improvement) and collaborative attacks (GEOMINER: 20% improvement over CoT)
Sophisticated analysis of subtle leakage mechanisms (mirror/reflection cases, tool-assisted reasoning)
Demonstrates practical threat: models outperform non-experts by 15-21× on average error distance
Honest evaluation of defense mechanisms, identifying fundamental limitations rather than overstating weak solutions
Well-executed research with clear presentation, logical flow, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited geographic scope: all 500 images from California only; generalization to other US regions and international settings is untested and likely problematic given regional differences in architecture, vegetation, and infrastructure

Unresolved ethical concerns: dataset contains real residential locations with identifiable features (house numbers, license plates); unclear if DOXBENCH will be publicly released and what privacy protections would be in place for residents
Limited technical novelty: core techniques are applications of existing work (Chain-of-Thought, cooperative inference); CLUEMINER uses straightforward LLM-based categorization
Moderate dataset scale: 500 images across 3 risk levels and 6 cities is limited for robust benchmarking; street-level accuracy only achieves 37-42 correct predictions at best

GLARE metric practical interpretation unclear: while information-theoretic foundation is sound, correlation with actual attacker capability needs empirical validation; choices (geometric mean, flat-earth approximation) justified informally
Incomplete comparison with concurrent work: references [21], [22], [3], [4], [5] studying similar problems but lacks head-to-head quantitative evaluation

Limited human baseline: only 5 CS undergraduates (non-diverse expertise); 300-second time limit unrealistic for dedicated adversaries; no comparison with expert geolocation specialists (GeoGuessr players)
Mirror case analysis underdeveloped: only 46 images; dramatic performance variations (O3: 11.57km vs. LLAMA: 288.64km AED) lack mechanistic explanation
CLUEMINER convergence not fully analyzed: ordering/initialization sensitivity not discussed; reproducibility concerns due to non-deterministic behavior

Defense mechanisms are weak: image perturbation shown to fail with no viable alternative; prompt-based filtering balances poorly between utility and safety; guardrail-based (LLAMA GUARD4) completely fails
Threat model assumptions underexplored: unrestricted API access assumed; cost barriers, rate-limiting, and potential API blocking downplayed
Limited analysis of WHY models differ: paper shows WHICH models are better but not architectural/training factors driving differences; limited insights for privacy-aware model design
Missing key ablations: visual content vs. internal knowledge contribution unclear; prompt engineering sensitivity not studied; image resolution impact not analyzed
Privacy level annotation lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics; L1/L2 and L2/L3 boundaries may be subjective
